statement: In obtuse-angled triangles the square on the side subtending the obtuse angle is greater than the squares on the sides containing the obtuse angle by twice the rectangle contained by one of the sides about the obtuse angle, namely that on which the   perpendicular falls, and the straight line cut off outside by the perpendicular towards the obtuse angle.
heath_proof: Let ABC be an obtuse-angled triangle having the angle BAC obtuse, and let BD be drawn from the point B perpendicular to CA produced;  I say that the square on BC is greater than the squares on BA, AC by twice the rectangle contained by CA, AD. For, since the straight line CD has been cut at random at the point A, the square on DC is equal to the squares on CA, AD and twice the rectangle contained by CA, AD. [II. 4] Let the square on DB be added to each; therefore the squares on CD, DB are equal to the squares on CA, AD, DB and twice the rectangle CA, AD. But the square on CB is equal to the squares on CD, DB, for the angle at D is right; [I. 47] and the square on AB is equal to the squares on AD, DB; [I. 47]therefore the square on CB is equal to the squares on CA, AB and twice the rectangle contained by CA, AD; so that the square on CB is greater than the squares on CA, AB by twice the rectangle contained by CA, AD.

**Statement:** In obtuse-angled triangles the square on the side subtending the obtuse angle is greater than the squares on the sides containing the obtuse angle by twice the rectangle contained by one of the sides about the obtuse angle, namely that on which the   perpendicular falls, and the straight line cut off outside by the perpendicular towards the obtuse angle.

**Step 1.** Let ABC be an obtuse-angled triangle having the angle BAC obtuse. Produce CA beyond A (P2), and from the point B draw BD perpendicular to CA produced (1.12), meeting it at D. Since BD is a perpendicular, the angles BDC and BDA are right (D1.10).

**Step 2.** The foot D lies on CA produced beyond A, that is, outside the triangle on the side of the obtuse angle. For if D coincided with A, the angle BAC would be right, whereas it is obtuse, i.e. greater than a right angle (D1.11); and if D lay on CA itself or on AC produced beyond C, then in the triangle BAD the angle BDA would be right and the angle BAD would be the obtuse angle BAC itself, so that two angles of the triangle BAD would together not be less than two right angles, contrary to 1.17. Hence D falls beyond A, CD is one straight line cut at the point A, and AD is the straight line cut off outside the triangle by the perpendicular towards the obtuse angle.

**Step 3.** Since the straight line CD has been cut at random at the point A, the square on DC is equal to the squares on CA, AD and twice the rectangle contained by CA, AD (2.4).

**Step 4.** Let the square on DB be added to each (CN2); therefore the squares on CD, DB are equal to the squares on CA, AD, DB and twice the rectangle contained by CA, AD.

**Step 5.** Since the angle BDC is right, the triangle BDC is right-angled, so the square on CB is equal to the squares on CD, DB (1.47); and likewise, since the angle BDA is right, the square on AB is equal to the squares on AD, DB (1.47).

**Step 6.** Therefore the square on CB, being equal to the squares on CD, DB (Step 5), is equal to the squares on CA, AD, DB and twice the rectangle CA, AD (Step 4, CN1); and since the squares on AD, DB are together equal to the square on AB (Step 5), the square on CB is equal to the squares on CA, AB and twice the rectangle contained by CA, AD (CN1).

**Step 7.** Hence the square on CB, the side subtending the obtuse angle, is greater than the squares on CA, AB, the sides containing the obtuse angle, by twice the rectangle contained by CA, the side on which the perpendicular falls, and AD, the straight line cut off outside by the perpendicular towards the obtuse angle. Q.E.D.
